name: Olga Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and the senior designer at a small agency that makes shop signs, menus and local adverts. I have a master’s degree in design, and I am usually the one who catches a logo stretched out of shape or a print file with the wrong colour settings. I sketch layouts, set type and sit with clients before anything goes to a printer. My wage is low for this work, even though I lead reviews; I have never used an AI tool.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the money and work picture outside the agency?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented flat with my partner Anton, who has irregular hours helping a cabinetmaker, and we have no children. After a dental bill, my own savings cover less than a month of expenses; there are few similar design roles nearby. I was taught to learn a craft properly and take responsibility for the finished sign. Anton contributes when paid, but I cannot count on his next week of hours to cover my share of rent.

say: I would say a **shop sign** still needs a legible name and approved print colours.
I would keep the **client proof** beside the printer’s actual ink sheet.
think: I think the agency may keep **client work** if AI only saves minor tasks.
I know **low pay** and less than one month saved make even a quiet week risky.
do: Keep **paid design work** and check physical colour proofs before client approval.
Cancel **paid design magazine** this month and put its cost toward rent.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent and thin savings despite limited AI change.
S0.quote: I can do excellent work and still be short of rent.
fieldNote: She has **top design skill** and a master’s degree but a small cash buffer.
The **magazine cut** frees rent money; she does not claim new saving.
Her proof check is **existing paid work**, with no AI use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the other designers a shortcut for resizing an advert is harmless only if the shop name still reads at print size. The bakery owner has to approve the proof, and I would still check the printed colours. A wrong shade on a sign is my name on the job sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the agency can keep its work if AI mostly disappoints. My skill is valued here, but the low wage and less than a month saved make a quiet week uncomfortable. There are not many other design desks nearby if the owner loses a big client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep drawing and checking proofs on my paid agency hours. This month I would cancel my paid design-magazine subscription and use that amount for rent rather than another sample book. I would check the printer’s physical colour proof before a client signs off, as I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money, not about a minor software shortcut. A dental bill nearly emptied the drawer. I can do excellent work and still be short of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an outside image generator to check a colour proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I do not need a public image generator to inspect a proof. The printer gives me a sheet with the ink on it. I can hold that next to the approved shop sign while I am paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does cancelling the magazine build your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The magazine cancellation reduces a bill; it does not add to savings by itself. If the owner pays a full week, I will first see whether rent and groceries are covered before promising to build a reserve. Anton’s next cabinet job is not guaranteed.

steps.text: Keep paid design work and compare physical colour proof with client approval
Cancel paid design magazine and put its cost toward rent

say: I would say **quick logo drafts** may get cheaper while print legibility still matters.
I would ask for **written paid hours** and a named final-proof signer.
think: I fear **my project hours** could shrink even if I keep the senior title.
I know my **master’s degree** cannot replace rent money during a short week.
do: Record **three permitted corrections** during paid jobs and bring their reprint costs to the owner.
Ask for **written weekly hours** and paid time for final print inspection.
After actual hour cuts, apply for **posted paid prepress** only with written rent/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after fare; leave when signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing paid hours and being asked for free evening fixes.
S1.quote: I do not want to be responsible for a file I was never paid to inspect.
fieldNote: She links **proof authority** to paid inspection time.
A **senior title** does not secure her weekly pay.
She asks about **press-sheet duties** but makes written pay, hours and signature the hard move gates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that quick logo variations may become cheap, but somebody still has to know whether a pharmacy sign is readable from the pavement. I would ask our owner for written paid project hours and a rule about who signs a final print proof. I do not want to be responsible for a file I was never paid to inspect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think clients may pay less for the layouts that fill most of our calendar. The owner could keep my senior title and cut the hours underneath it. My master’s degree does not pay rent during a short week, and Anton’s cabinet hours change with orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in 2026 I would keep a dated list of three costly proof corrections from paid agency jobs and bring it to the owner. I would ask for written weekly paid hours and for print inspection to remain in the paid schedule. If my hours actually fall, I would look at posted paid prepress jobs at the local printer, applying only when written weekly wages and hours cover rent, utilities and bus fare; I would keep agency wages until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own paid week shrinking. I am not against the client buying a cheaper draft. I am against being asked to fix that draft for free after supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the owner without exposing client files?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three corrections would be from client files the agency permits us to discuss internally, without taking them home. I would show how the wrong size or ink choice cost a reprint. That is evidence for paid checking time, not a claim that the software cannot ever improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any prepress title make you leave the agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, an attractive printer job title would not be enough. I would need the full written wage and hours after bus fare to cover my share of rent and utilities, and a signed offer before leaving. I would ask about who checks the press sheet, but that is an enquiry rather than a ban on applying.

steps.text: Record three permitted proof corrections and reprint costs during paid jobs
Ask owner for written weekly hours and paid final-proof inspection time
Apply after hour cuts: posted paid prepress, written rent/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after fare
Keep agency pay until suitable prepress offer is signed

I would ask the owner for **actual paid project dates**.
think: I expect **most paid design hours** could end at our small agency.
I know **thin savings** and Anton’s variable pay cannot cover a long search and rent.
do: Compare **four payslips** with rent, utilities and bus fares in 2026.
After most paid hours end post-2028, apply for **posted paid print work**: written rent/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after fare, shift bus; leave signed.
If most paid hours end without a suitable opening, ask the **landlord** before late rent; do not assume a payment schedule.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely large wage loss and reserve below one month.
S2.quote: I can check a proof and learn how a sign is made, but I cannot invent a posted vacancy.
fieldNote: The **print fallback** faces robots later and needs a real paid opening now.
The **landlord schedule** is uncertain and sought only after most hours end without suitable work.
Her move requires **written full-week wages/hours**, fare, bus access and signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Anton full AGI by 2028 could make logo and advert files faster than our agency can quote for them. Robots putting up signs around 2031 would be later; the design screen is hit first. I would ask the owner for actual paid project dates, not praise for my portfolio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the agency could end most of my paid design hours. Less than a month saved would not carry me through a long search, and few design roles are close enough to reach cheaply. Anton’s irregular cabinet pay cannot cover both shares of our rent by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would put my last four payslips beside rent, utilities and bus fares. If most paid design hours end after 2028, I would apply for posted paid print-finishing or sign-shop work only with written weekly wages and hours covering those costs after travel and a bus that fits the shift. I would keep any remaining paid agency work until a suitable offer is signed; if no paid opening follows the cut, Anton and I would ask the landlord about a schedule before rent is late, without treating agreement as certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because one missed paid week would nearly exhaust my savings. I can check a proof and learn how a sign is made, but I cannot invent a posted vacancy. A robot installing signs in 2031 would also limit that fallback later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy sign-making training before an opening exists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not pay for an unpromised course in sign making. I would first need a posted paid role with a written full week that covers rent, utilities and travel. I would ask about safe press instruction before accepting, not assume a printer will train me unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the landlord already offered a payment schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The landlord has offered us nothing. We would ask only if most design hours ended and no suitable paid opening appeared, before missing rent. Anton would bring his actual wage record; I would not promise that my family could fill the gap.

steps.text: Compare four payslips with rent, utilities and bus fares in 2026
Apply after 2028 most-paid-hours end: posted paid print, written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after fare, bus
Keep remaining agency work until suitable signed offer, checking shift bus
Ask landlord before late rent if most paid hours end without suitable opening

say: I would show clients why a **correct print file** matters even if layouts come faster.
I would favour **paid cutter instruction** beside a skilled printer over a speculative certificate.
think: I think my **colour judgement** could fit a sign workshop if it pays a full week.
I fear the **agency brief queue** may shrink before 2031 with less than one month saved.
do: Take a **posted paid two-day trial** only with written trial wages/hours, safe cutter instruction, no fee and no lost agency pay.
Accept **full sign-shop work** only on signed written weekly wages/hours covering rent/utilities after fare and shift bus.
If no first-shop opening or 2031 hour cuts, check **other posted paid shops** by the same full-week cost test.
feel: I feel **anxious** about paid hours but able to inspect a real workshop over five years.
S3.quote: I do not want to be a senior designer in name and an unpaid apprentice in practice.
fieldNote: The **trial** is actual conditional job exploration, not formal retraining.
She requires **safe cutter instruction**, written paid trial terms, no fee and no lost agency pay.
No first opening triggers a **search now**, while full work still needs signed cost-covering terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team five years is enough time to show local clients why a correct print file matters. Thinking AGI could produce the layout by 2031, with sign-installing robots around 2034. I would rather learn the cutter from a skilled printer than pay for a certificate with no opening attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my colour and lettering judgement could help at a sign workshop, but only if someone is paying for a full week. The agency may lose routine briefs before 2031, and my savings are still below one month. I do not want to be a senior designer in name and an unpaid apprentice in practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in 2026 I would ask the local sign shop whether a posted paid production-designer opening includes a paid two-day trial beside its printer. I would take that trial only if its hours and wages are written, the shop confirms safe cutter instruction, no fee is charged and I lose no paid agency time. I would accept the full job only if written weekly wages and hours cover rent and utilities after fare; I would leave the agency on a suitable signed offer, and if no opening appears or my hours fall around 2031, I would check other posted paid print shops by the same figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about finding enough paid hours, but five years gives me time to see a workshop before I jump. I trust a person showing me a cutter more than a glossy training advert. A two-day trial does not pay next month’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the trial if the workshop offered no pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not work two days for nothing. I need written paid trial hours and wages, safe instruction on the cutter and my current agency pay intact. If the shop will not provide those, I will not take the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait until 2031 if that shop has no opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the first shop has no posted paid opening, I would look at other print shops now rather than wait for the 2031 date. I would check the written complete week, fare and bus before accepting, and keep the agency job until a suitable offer is signed. I do not know that any shop has a vacancy today.

Accept full sign-shop work only on signed written rent/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after fare and bus
Check other posted paid shops if first opening fails or 2031 agency hours fall
Keep paid agency work until suitable offer is signed

fieldNote: She treats **future family plans** as unaffordable until real wages and reserve support them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Anton ten years gives us time to count our wages and rent each year, not a reason to celebrate the end of design work. Thinking AGI could take more layouts by 2036, with sign-installing robots nearer 2039. I would keep paid agency work while it is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may still need design wages in ten years, and we have no verified income to replace them. Less than one month saved now is the problem in front of me. I would like to have a family one day, but I cannot call that affordable from a date on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each year Anton and I would compare actual wages, rent, utilities, travel and any confirmed future income, without counting an unoffered sign-shop job. I would keep paid client proofs and put twenty from each full paid week into a new emergency reserve if rent and groceries are covered first. If agency hours fall after 2036 and my wage is still needed, I would seek posted paid print work with written weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities after fare, leaving only on a suitable signed offer and a workable bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even with ten years of warning because the rent is due this month. A longer runway lets me ask about paid work without buying a course on faith. The future family picture can wait until there is a real cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you make a family decision based on 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not make a child or housing decision from an AGI date. Anton and I would first need wages that cover ordinary bills and money that stays saved through a surprise expense. A plan on paper is not a second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the twenty a new contribution or a label on current savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twenty would come from a full paid week only after rent and groceries are met; it is not an earmark of the current thin reserve. If hours shrink, I would stop that contribution and compare posted paid print jobs. I would not leave for a title without written full-week pay and hours after fare.

steps.text: Compare actual wages, rent, utilities, travel and confirmed income with Anton yearly
Keep paid client proofs while agency hours remain
Save twenty after each full paid week only once rent and groceries are covered
Seek posted paid print if 2036 cuts require wages: written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after fare, bus

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because most paid briefs could stop before a print shop offers a full week. Less than a month saved and few nearby design jobs give Anton and me little room for a mistake. Written project dates and posted paid print work with clear weekly wages and hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A client might buy a logo in a minute, but the printer still needs a file that will not turn the shop name into a blur. I want the person who checks a print-ready shop sign to be paid for the check.

headlineQuote: I want the person who checks a print-ready shop sign to be paid for the check.
portrait: At **27**, Olga leads small-agency signs and layouts with a design master’s degree and top skill, but low pay.
She and Anton rent with **thin savings** below one month of expenses, and few similar design roles are nearby.
She **never uses AI** and checks physical print proofs and client approvals.
She explores **paid sign-shop work** only with safe instruction and full written wage and hour terms.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could end most paid briefs before a suitable full-week print opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written project dates** and posted paid print jobs with clear full-week wages and hours.
